blocks.text: About 60 kilometres north of Mary, in the sands of the Karakum, lies a low mound that local people call *Goňur depe*. Its excavators translate the name as **grey hill**; *depe* is a hill or mound. Four thousand years ago it was one of the largest towns of Central Asia, in the delta of the Murgab river, in the land later called Margiana.

**The dig.** In 1972 the archaeologist Viktor Sarianidi picked up the first pieces of pottery from the surface of the mound. He began to excavate in 1974 and went on, season after season, until 2013, and other teams have worked there since. The site covers about 55 hectares. On the most common dating, people lived there from roughly 2400 to 1600 BCE, in the Bronze Age, and Gonur is seen as the main centre of what archaeologists call the Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex, or the Oxus civilization.

**What was found.** In the northern part stood a large building, often called the palace, inside a double wall, with temples, courtyards for rituals and water reservoirs around it. A catalogue of the Berlin museum that showed the finds in 2018 points out the water pipes laid underground. West of the town lies a cemetery of more than three thousand graves. The richest tombs held gold, silver and bronze, objects of ivory brought from far away, and mosaics that once covered walls and wooden boxes, like those known from Mesopotamia. In one grave lay a four-wheeled wooden wagon with bronze rims, buried with a horse and dated to about 2250 BCE.
**Why it ended.** The town was most likely abandoned when the Murgab shifted its course to the west and the delta dried out around it. Without the river, the oasis became desert.

**What it means.** Sarianidi saw the fire altars and temples of Gonur as an early form of the rituals of Zoroastrianism, and its people as newcomers from elsewhere. Other archaeologists, among them C. C. Lamberg-Karlovsky, describe the origin of this culture as much debated: whether it came from outside or grew from local roots is still argued, and the link with Zoroastrianism is one hypothesis among several. What is not in doubt is that Gonur had contacts with distant lands, from Mesopotamia to the Indus valley.

blocks.title: Two old towns near Mary
blocks.text: Gonur is far older than Merv, the oasis city of [A2 unit 3](a2-u03-culture): by the time Merv grew up, Gonur had been sand for a thousand years and more. Both are in Mary province ([A2 unit 8](a2-u08-culture)).
With this unit's postpositions, you can read this:

blocks.en: Gonur Depe is in Mary province, out in the desert. Four thousand years ago there was a big town here. In the middle of the town there was a palace, and outside it there were two walls. Scholars have been coming here since 1974. They have found gold, silver and an ancient wagon here.

vocab.en: Margiana, the ancient land around Merv

questions.q: When was Gonur Depe lived in, on the most common dating?
questions.explain: Gonur belongs to the Bronze Age: roughly 2400 to 1600 BCE.

questions.q: Why was the town most likely abandoned?
options: the Murgab river changed its course
questions.explain: The river shifted west, and the delta around the town dried out.

questions.q: In the reading, what was outside the palace?
questions.explain: *Onuň daşynda iki diwar bardy*: outside it there were two walls.
